title: Practice Exam 4
description: A fourth full-length 36-question simulated California Class C knowledge exam. Challenging level.

questions.question: Your car begins to hydroplane on standing water at highway speed. You should:
choices: Ease off the accelerator, keep the wheel steady, and avoid braking until traction returns
Brake firmly to slow the car at once
Accelerate to push through the water
Steer sharply toward the shoulder
questions.explanation: When tires ride up on water, gently lift off the gas and hold the wheel straight—braking or sharp steering can cause a skid. Best of all, slow down in the rain to prevent hydroplaning.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Hydroplaning

questions.question: On an icy bridge posted at 50 mph, driving 50 mph could still get you cited because:
choices: The Basic Speed Law forbids any speed unsafe for conditions, even at the limit
Bridges always have a 25 mph limit
Speed limits don't apply on bridges
Only trucks must slow on ice
questions.explanation: The posted number is a maximum for ideal conditions. On ice the safe (and legal) speed may be far lower; exceeding it violates the Basic Speed Law.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Basic Speed Law

questions.question: A sign reads 'SLOWER TRAFFIC KEEP RIGHT.' If you are moving slower than the cars around you, you must:
choices: Move into the right lane to let faster traffic pass
Stay where you are but slow down further
Speed up to match the fastest car
Move to the left lane to get out of the way
questions.explanation: This sign directs slower drivers to keep right so faster traffic can pass on the left. Lingering in a left lane while slower than surrounding traffic impedes flow.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Lane Use Signs

questions.question: You are on a freeway off-ramp and see a red 'WRONG WAY' sign facing you. This means:
choices: You are heading the wrong direction; stop, pull over if needed, and turn around safely
The ramp ahead is closed
You may continue if no cars are coming
Make an immediate U-turn right where you are
questions.explanation: 'WRONG WAY' warns you're about to drive against traffic, often onto a freeway. Stop, get out of the path of oncoming cars, and turn around—do not continue.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Regulatory Signs

questions.question: Two cars meet on a steep, narrow mountain road too tight to pass, one heading up and one down. Who must yield by backing up?
choices: The car heading downhill backs up; the uphill car has the right of way
The car heading uphill backs up
The larger vehicle backs up
Whoever is closer to a wide spot, regardless of direction
questions.explanation: The downhill driver yields and backs up, because a vehicle backing uphill has better control than one backing down. The uphill car keeps the right of way.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Mountain Driving

questions.question: You have a stop sign; the cross street does not. After stopping, you see a car approaching on the cross street. You must:
choices: Wait and yield to the cross traffic, even though you stopped first
Proceed because you already came to a complete stop
Proceed because you arrived before the other car
Expect the cross traffic to slow for you
questions.explanation: Your stop sign only controls your road. Cross traffic without a stop sign has the right of way; you must yield until it is safe to enter.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Stop Signs

questions.question: On a one-way street with three lanes, you may move between lanes:
choices: Freely when clear, since all lanes travel the same direction—still signal and check blind spots
Never; lane changes are banned on one-way streets
Only by coming to a stop first
Only at intersections
questions.explanation: All lanes go the same way on a one-way street, so you may change lanes when clear. The usual rules still apply: signal, check mirrors, and check the blind spot.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — One-Way Streets

questions.question: Weaving rapidly between lanes in heavy traffic to get ahead:
choices: Sharply raises crash risk and usually saves little or no time
Is the safest way to make progress
Is recommended when you are running late
Is legal only on freeways
questions.explanation: Frequent aggressive lane changes greatly increase the chance of a collision while rarely getting you there faster. Pick a lane and keep a steady, safe pace.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Safe Lane Use

questions.question: Compared with dry pavement, your following distance on a wet or gravel road should be:
choices: Longer, because traction is reduced and stopping takes more distance
Shorter, to keep up with traffic
Exactly the same three seconds
Whatever feels comfortable
questions.explanation: Reduced traction lengthens stopping distance, so increase your gap well beyond three seconds on wet, icy, or loose surfaces.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Following Distance in Poor Conditions

questions.question: Maintaining a 'space cushion' on all sides of your car is valuable mainly because it:
choices: Gives you time and room to see and avoid sudden hazards
Lets you legally drive faster
Improves fuel economy
Makes parking easier
questions.explanation: Open space ahead, behind, and beside you provides escape routes and reaction time when another driver makes a mistake.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Managing Space

questions.question: After a lawful DUI arrest, a driver refuses both the breath and blood tests. The likely result is:
choices: An automatic license suspension plus added penalties, regardless of the DUI outcome
No penalty, since testing is optional
Only a small fine
Dismissal of the DUI charge
questions.explanation: Implied consent means refusing a required chemical test after a lawful arrest brings a mandatory suspension and additional penalties, separate from the DUI case.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Refusing a Chemical Test

questions.question: A commercial driver operating a big rig may not drive with a BAC at or above:
questions.explanation: Commercial drivers face a stricter 0.04% limit—half the 0.08% for regular drivers. (Under-21 drivers face 0.01%.)
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Commercial Driver BAC

questions.question: A flashing yellow beacon is mounted above a 'SCHOOL' sign and is flashing. This tells you:
choices: A school zone is active—slow to the posted school-zone speed and watch for children
School is closed today
You may not enter the street
Stop completely until the beacon turns off
questions.explanation: A flashing yellow beacon means the reduced school-zone speed is in effect and children are likely present. Slow down and be ready to stop.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — School Zones

questions.question: You are driving past a row of parked cars near a school when a small child runs out from between two of them. Your best protection against this was to:
choices: Already be driving slowly and scanning the gaps between parked cars
Honk continuously while driving past
Drive faster to clear the area quickly
Stay centered in your lane at the speed limit
questions.explanation: Slowing down and watching the spaces between parked cars near a school gives you time to react when a child suddenly appears. Speed and noise are no substitute for caution.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Watching for Children

questions.question: A traffic light is green, but a police officer at the intersection signals you to stop. The correct action is to:
choices: Stop—an officer's direction overrides the signal
Follow the green light
Proceed slowly past the officer
Stop only if the cross street is busy
questions.explanation: An officer directing traffic has authority over signals and signs. Always obey the officer, even when it contradicts the light.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Obeying Officers

questions.question: Firefighters are working a fire and a hose lies across the road. You may drive over the hose only:
choices: If a fire official directs you to
If you are in a hurry
If no firefighters are looking
If the hose appears flat
questions.explanation: It is illegal to drive over an unprotected fire hose without permission from a fire department official. Wait or find another route.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Fire Scenes

questions.question: On a rural road with no sidewalk, a pedestrian is walking ahead in your lane facing you. You should:
choices: Slow down and move over to give them plenty of room as you pass
Hold your speed and lane position
Honk repeatedly until they leave the road
Expect them to step into the ditch
questions.explanation: Where there's no sidewalk, give pedestrians extra space and reduce speed when passing. They have a right to use the roadway safely.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Sharing the Road with Pedestrians

questions.question: You've parallel parked on a busy street. Before opening your driver's door, you must:
choices: Check mirrors and look back for cars and bicyclists approaching from behind
Open it quickly to avoid blocking traffic
Trust that traffic will steer around your door
Open it halfway as a warning to others
questions.explanation: Opening a door into the path of a cyclist or car ('dooring') causes serious crashes and is illegal. Check mirrors and look back before opening, and don't leave it open longer than needed.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Opening Doors Safely

questions.question: A curb is painted yellow. You may:
choices: Stop only long enough to load or unload passengers or freight, within any posted time limit
Park there all day
Never stop there for any reason
Park there only with a disabled placard
questions.explanation: Yellow curbs are loading zones—stop briefly to load or unload, observing the posted time limit, and stay with the vehicle if required.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Colored Curbs

questions.question: You stop briefly in a disabled-parking space to wait for someone, without a placard. This is:
choices: Illegal—these spaces require a valid placard or plate even for a brief stop
Legal because you stayed in the car
Legal for stops under five minutes
Legal after business hours
questions.explanation: Disabled spaces (and the striped access aisles beside them) may be used only by vehicles displaying a valid placard or plate—no exceptions for short waits.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Disabled Parking

questions.question: You are in the right freeway lane and cars are merging from an on-ramp ahead. The cooperative, safe action is to:
choices: Move one lane left if it's safe, or adjust speed to open a gap for merging traffic
Speed up to close the gap and block them
Stop in your lane to let them all in
Move onto the right shoulder to pass the ramp
questions.explanation: Help merging traffic by moving over when you safely can, or adjusting speed to leave a gap. Blocking or stopping disrupts the flow and causes crashes.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Freeway Merging

questions.question: On a long, monotonous freeway drive you notice your eyes getting heavy and your mind wandering. The only real fix is to:
choices: Stop to rest, nap, or switch drivers
Turn the radio up loud
Open the window and drive faster to finish sooner
Drink coffee and keep going for hours
questions.explanation: Drowsiness is as dangerous as alcohol. Tricks like loud music or cold air wear off quickly; the only safe remedy is to stop and rest or let someone else drive.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Fatigue and Driving

questions.question: A text message arrives while you're driving and it seems urgent. The legal and safest choice is to:
choices: Leave it until you can pull over and stop in a safe place
Reply quickly while stopped at the next red light
Read it now but don't type a reply
Hold the phone low and glance between it and the road
questions.explanation: Texting while driving is illegal for everyone, including at red lights. If a message can't wait, pull over and stop somewhere safe before handling it.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Texting While Driving

questions.question: Which statement about 'multitasking' while driving is accurate?
choices: The brain rapidly switches tasks rather than truly doing two at once, so driving suffers
Experienced drivers can safely text and drive
Hands-free use removes all distraction
Practice makes multitasking while driving safe
questions.explanation: People don't truly multitask; the brain switches between tasks, leaving gaps where you miss what's happening on the road. Give driving your full attention.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Cognitive Distraction

questions.question: Your light is green but traffic ahead is backed up across the intersection so you couldn't fully clear it. You should:
choices: Wait behind the line until there's room on the far side—don't block the intersection
Enter on the green and stop in the middle if needed
Edge in to hold your position
Proceed because a green always means go
questions.explanation: Never enter an intersection you can't clear ('blocking the box'). Wait behind the limit line until space opens on the other side, even with a green light.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Intersections

questions.question: Approaching a signal that has been green a long time ('stale green'), the best habit is to:
choices: Be prepared for it to turn yellow—cover the brake and be ready to stop
Speed up to get through before it changes
Assume it will stay green
Close your following gap to the car ahead
questions.explanation: A light that's been green a while may change as you arrive. Anticipate a yellow, ease off the gas, and be ready to stop safely rather than racing through.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Traffic Signal Lights

questions.question: Over the lane you're in, a lane-control signal changes from a green arrow to a steady red X. You must:
choices: Move out of that lane as soon as it is safe—the lane is closing to your direction
Stop in the lane and wait
Speed up to pass through it
Ignore it; it applies only to trucks
questions.explanation: A red X means the lane is no longer open to you; merge safely into an open lane. A green downward arrow means the lane is open for use.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Lane Use Signals

questions.question: You have a green light, but a pedestrian against the signal is already in the crosswalk in your path. You should:
choices: Yield and avoid the pedestrian, even though they are crossing illegally
Proceed because you have the right of way
Honk and drive through at speed
Accelerate to pass before they reach your lane
questions.explanation: Right of way is something you give, not take. Even when a pedestrian errs, you must do everything reasonable to avoid hitting them.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Pedestrian Safety

questions.question: Diagonal yellow-and-black stripes painted across a paved area beside the travel lane mark:
choices: A fixed obstruction or median you must not drive onto
An extra parking area
A passing lane
A bicycle lane
questions.explanation: These diagonal stripes (often a 'gore' area or median nose) mark a fixed obstruction or no-drive zone. Stay in the marked travel lane and don't cross them.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Pavement Markings

questions.question: You park facing downhill on a street with NO curb. Turn the front wheels:
choices: Toward the edge of the road
Toward the center of the road
Away from the edge of the road
Straight, relying on the transmission
questions.explanation: Downhill with no curb, point the wheels toward the road's edge so a runaway car rolls off the road rather than into traffic. Set the parking brake and leave it in park (or in gear).
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Parking on Hills

questions.question: You are driving through an alley behind some shops. The speed limit, unless otherwise posted, is:
choices: 15 mph
20 mph
25 mph
10 mph
questions.explanation: The speed limit in any alley is 15 mph. Watch closely for pedestrians and vehicles backing out of driveways and loading areas.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — 15 mph Speed Limits

questions.question: Approaching a sharp curve, the correct technique is to:
choices: Slow down before you enter the curve, then accelerate gently through it
Brake hard in the middle of the curve
Enter fast and coast around
Hold a high constant speed throughout
questions.explanation: Reduce speed before entering the curve, then gently accelerate as you go through it for stability. Braking mid-curve can break traction and cause a skid.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Driving Through Curves

questions.question: You are sober, but a passenger is drinking from an open can of beer as you drive. This is:
choices: Illegal—no one may have an open container of alcohol in the passenger area
Legal because the driver is sober
Legal because it is the passenger, not the driver
Legal if the passenger is over 21
questions.explanation: The open-container law bans open alcohol in the passenger compartment for everyone, including passengers. The driver can be cited even while sober.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Open Container Law

questions.question: A bicyclist ahead extends their left arm straight out. This signals that the cyclist intends to:
choices: Turn left
Turn right
Stop
Speed up
questions.explanation: A straight-out left arm means a left turn. A left arm bent up means right turn, and a left arm bent down means stopping. Yield and give the cyclist room.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Bicycle Hand Signals

questions.question: Good freeway drivers scan far down the road, about:
choices: 10 to 15 seconds ahead, while also checking mirrors and sides
Only the bumper of the car directly ahead
Only the speedometer
Only the lane lines beside the car
questions.explanation: Looking 10–15 seconds ahead lets you spot brake lights, debris, and slowdowns early, while frequent mirror and side checks keep you aware of nearby vehicles.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Scanning the Road

questions.question: You signal to change lanes, but a car accelerates into the space and ends up in your blind spot. You should:
choices: Stay in your lane and wait until the space is clearly open again
Change lanes anyway and let them brake
Speed up and cut in ahead of them
Move over gradually to push them back
questions.explanation: Abort the lane change if someone fills the gap or sits in your blind spot. Adjust your speed and wait for a clearly open, visible space before moving over.
questions.handbook_reference: California Driver's Handbook — Blind Spots
